newsitem.title: USA: Short circuit blamed for cruise liner fire.
newsitem.headline: Short circuit blamed for cruise liner fire.

text.p: Cunard Line Ltd said Monday that an electrical short circuit had caused a weekend fire on board the Vistafjord cruise ship that left one crewman dead and at least two other people injured.
The company also said that fire damage to the ship's laundry and minor smoke damage in some passenger areas had caused it to cancel the cruise.

All 569 passengers on board the liner were to receive full reimbursement for their trips, as well as a $1,000 per person travel credit to be applied to a future cruise on Vistafjord or Cunard's Queen Elizabeth 2 or Royal Viking Sun.

The company chartered aircraft to fly passengers from Freeport, Bahamas, where the Vistafjord was forced to dock after the fire, with some passengers scheduled to travel to Miami and then home on Monday and others expected to leave the ship on Tuesday.

Vistafjord has been docked in Freeport since early Sunday, when a fire detected shortly after it left Fort Lauderdale, Florida, forced the ship to abort a trans-Atlantic cruise to Funchal on the Portuguese island of Madeira.
Stephen Moller, identified as a German waiter in his 20s, was found unconscious in a cabin after the fire broke out and died Sunday morning at a Freeport hospital.

New York-based Cunard, owner of the 627-foot (190-metre) Bahamian-registered vessel, said the electrical short circuit in the Vistafjord's laundry's chemical dispensing equipment had caused the blaze. Another crew member suffered a broken ankle and a passenger broke an arm. Cunard is a subsidiary of the Norwegian shipbuilding group Kvaerner ASA.
Cunard said the ship would be repaired during an upcoming, previously scheduled dry-docking in Malta April 21-May 5, returning to its scheduled service after May 5.

Freeport harbor officials had said earlier Monday that the hundreds of passengers who remained on board the Vistafjord were comfortable. "It's a good thing it happened early while it was fairly close to land," David Johnson, executive vice president of the Grand Bahama Tourism Board, said.

The pre-dawn fire had forced hundreds of passengers to gather on deck at emergency stations. Other ships in the area were diverted to the scene in case evacuation was needed, but the fire did not spread beyond the ship's laundry. The fire was put out shortly after the Vistafjord arrived in Freeport.
